record.paper_title: Recent Results and Open Problems in Evolutionary Multiobjective Optimization
record.original_question: Can self-adaptive or online-adaptive multi-objective evolutionary algorithms be made effectively parameterless by automatically choosing parameters such as mutation rate, crossover rate, population size, or encoding while using well-defined convergence criteria and population-behavior signals to guide the search?

evidence.quote: dream of creating a parameterless multi-objective evolutionary algorithm

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a multi-objective evolutionary algorithm (MOEA) designed to approximate the Pareto-optimal set of a vector optimization problem $\min_{x \in X} F(x) = (f_1(x), \ldots, f_m(x))$, where $m \ge 2$. Such algorithms typically depend on strategy parameters including the mutation rate, the crossover rate, the population size, and the choice of solution encoding. A self-adaptive (or online-adaptive) MOEA is one that modifies these parameters during the run using only information observable from the algorithm's own state, such as statistics of the current population (e.g. diversity, spread, hypervolume progress) and a well-defined numerical convergence criterion for multi-objective search.

Problem: Devise a self-adaptive / online-adaptive MOEA that is effectively parameterless, in the following sense:
1. Before the run, the user supplies no values for the mutation rate, crossover rate, population size, or encoding-related parameters; the algorithm chooses and updates all of them automatically.
2. The algorithm uses a rigorously defined convergence criterion for multi-objective optimization (addressing the difficulty that, unlike the single-objective case, there is no universally accepted notion of convergence for an approximation of the Pareto front) together with signals derived from observed population behavior to drive parameter adaptation and termination.
3. On a broad class of multi-objective test problems, the resulting parameterless algorithm matches or surpasses the quality of approximations produced by carefully hand-tuned MOEAs.

Either construct such an algorithm together with a proof or convincing empirical demonstration of property (3), or show that no algorithm satisfying (1)–(3) can exist under stated assumptions.
artifact.status_search_result: Self-adaptive MOEAs (e.g. SaMOEA/D, MOSA-EA, fuzzy-controlled memetic MOEAs) continue to be actively developed, and recent surveys still list automatic parameter control and well-defined multi-objective convergence criteria as ongoing challenges. No method has been recognized as a fully parameterless MOEA achieving competitive performance across problem classes, so the problem remains open.

status_evidence.title: A fuzzy system based self-adaptive memetic algorithm using population diversity control for evolutionary multi-objective optimization
status_evidence.snippet: Self-adaptive memetic algorithms with diversity control are still being proposed as a way to reduce manual parameter setting in MOEAs.
status_evidence.claim: Self-adaptive parameter control in MOEAs is an active and unresolved area of research.

status_evidence.title: Self-adaptation via Multi-objectivisation: An Empirical Study
status_evidence.snippet: MOSA-EA optimizes single-objective functions via multi-objectivisation, simultaneously evolving fitness and mutation rates.
status_evidence.claim: Recent work continues to propose self-adaptive evolutionary methods rather than declaring the parameterless MOEA goal achieved.

status_evidence.title: Self-adaptive MOEA/D for large-scale problems
status_evidence.snippet: Each subproblem adaptively chooses neighborhood size and genetic operator based on search history.
status_evidence.claim: Adaptive parameter control in decomposition-based MOEAs continues to be developed without yielding a universally parameterless MOEA.
